description:
Declare a remote function as a task, start a runtime with it registered, and
call it:

```mojo
from dista import Runtime, Task

def square(x: Int) -> Int:
    return x * x

comptime Square = Task[Int, Int, square]

def main() raises:
    var rt = Runtime[Square](workers=4)
    var r = rt.remote[Square](7)
    print(rt.get(r))  # 49
```

An actor keeps state between calls on a worker of its own:

```mojo
comptime CounterActor = Actor[Counter, Int, new_counter]
comptime Add = Method[CounterActor, Int, Int, add]

var rt = Runtime[CounterActor, Add](workers=2)
var c = rt.create[CounterActor](0)
var total = rt.call[Add](c, 5)  # an ObjectRef[Int]
rt.kill(c)
```

See DESIGN.md for how it works.

modules.summary: Where actor checkpoints live: objects under `DISTA_CHECKPOINT_URI`.
modules.description:
The URI is a local directory, a `file://` one, or anything objectstore
writes to, such as `s3://bucket/prefix`. A local directory only outlives the
worker that wrote it if the node that restarts the actor sees it too, so a
cluster needs a shared volume or object storage.

Each checkpoint is its own object, named for its actor and the number of
calls it covers, `<uri>/<actor ID in hex>/<calls>`, so a new one never
overwrites the one the head would restore from. The worker hosting the
actor deletes the ones before that one, those its predecessor left
included. A head that restarts restores each actor from its newest.

A checkpoint's bytes are, for each caller whose calls it includes, that
caller's number and the newest call's object ID, then the actor's state:
count u64, that many pairs of u64s, the state through the codec. Calls
resent after a head restart that it already includes aren't run again.

overloads.summary: `DISTA_CHECKPOINT_URI`, without a trailing slash; raises if unset.

overloads.signature: def checkpoint_location(actor: UInt64, calls: Int) -> String
overloads.summary: Where actor `actor`'s checkpoint after `calls` calls lives.
The calls covered by actor `actor`'s newest checkpoint, or -1.
The calls covered by each checkpoint actor `actor` has, in any order.

Writes a whole checkpoint, never part of one: after a head restart the newest is restored without anyone having said it was finished. An object store's put is whole already; a local file is written under a temporary name and renamed into place.
Deletes a checkpoint nothing will restore from; a failure only leaves it behind.

modules.summary: The driver's side of the protocol: submitting tasks, calling actors and getting results back from the head.
modules.description:
`Runtime` is the program's entry point: it starts the process in its role
and checks that what it's given is registered. `Client` is the part that
talks to the head, without the registry, so it can also run inside a
worker: a `CtxTask` gets one, and can call actors or submit tasks from
there. A worker's client connects with `ROLE_CLIENT`, which the head treats
as a driver, except that it doesn't keep a local-mode head alive.

A client checks only what it can know: that it didn't kill an actor it
calls. Whether the task, actor or method exists is the binary's: every
process runs the same registry, and the head refuses a peer that doesn't.

It returns at once; calls made before the actor is up wait for it.
If the constructor raises, every call fails with its error. With
`checkpoint_every` set, its state is checkpointed after every that
many calls.

overloads.summary: Destroys `actor` once its earlier calls have run, and frees its worker. Their results stay until released.

overloads.signature: def release[R: AnyType](mut self, r: ObjectRef[R])
overloads.summary: Says this driver is done with `r`.
overloads.description:
The result is freed, here, at the head and on its worker, once no
submitted task still needs it; a task already given `r` as input
still gets it. Releasing before the task has finished is fine: the
result is dropped when it arrives. `get(r)` raises from now on, and a
task submitted on `r` afterwards fails.

overloads.summary: Releases every ref in `refs`.
Asks the head what it holds. Frames that arrive first are kept.
Every task this driver submitted that has finished, with its timeline, since the last call. A head restart loses the spans it held and those of tasks running then.
Wall-clock nanoseconds, the clock the timeline uses: the start to give `span`.

overloads.summary: Where `r`'s result lives: a worker's `ip:port`, then its node-store file if it has one; "" if it came back with the reply. Waits for the task to finish.

structs.summary: A remote function that also gets a `Client`: from inside the task it can call actors, whose handles it was given, and submit tasks.
structs.description:
```mojo
def bump(mut c: Client, h: ActorHandle[CounterActor]) raises -> Int:
    var r = c.call[Add](h, 1)
    var n = c.get(r)
    c.release(r)
    return n

comptime Bump = CtxTask[ActorHandle[CounterActor], Int, bump]
```

A call from a task blocks that task until the answer comes; an actor
calling back into the worker that's waiting on it would deadlock, and
tasks never run on an actor's worker, so a task can't.

actor calls deadlocks, as it would with one thread per actor anywhere.

overloads.signature: def write_trace(path: String, spans: List[TaskSpan], mine: List[_DriverSpan] = List()) -> Int
overloads.summary: Writes finished tasks, and a driver's own spans, to `path` in Chrome's trace format, for Perfetto (ui.perfetto.dev) or chrome://tracing, and returns how many tasks it holds.
overloads.description:
Each worker is a process with two tracks: its tasks running, and its
tasks waiting for their inputs. The driver's spans are a process above
them. Times are microseconds from the first submission or driver span;
each run's arguments carry the head's waits too. A task without a name
is named by its wire ID.

overloads.summary: Splits `host:port`.
Connects to the head at `host:port`, retrying while it isn't up yet.
overloads.description:
In a cluster, processes start in any order: a worker's pod can come up
before the head's, or before its name resolves. This keeps trying for
`DISTA_CONNECT_TIMEOUT` seconds (default 60), then raises the last error.

The wait between tries starts at 10 ms and doubles to 250 ms: a head that
restarts is usually back within a fraction of a second, and a flat 250 ms
added that much to every recovery.

modules.summary: Turning task arguments and results into bytes and back.
modules.description:
`encode` and `decode` work on any type, chosen at compile time:

- built-in scalars, `Bool` and `String` have fixed encodings (little-endian
  fixed width; `String` is an 8-byte length then its UTF-8 bytes);
- arrow-mlake's `RecordBatch` is an 8-byte length then one Arrow IPC stream
  holding the schema and the batch, so columnar data crosses processes in
  Arrow's own format;
- a type that conforms to `Codec` encodes itself;
- any other struct is encoded field by field, in declaration order, by
  reflection.

Built-ins are recognised by `reflect[T].name()`, because `Int` or `String`
can't adopt a dista trait. `List` and other generic containers aren't
supported: reflection can't recover their element type. Wrap them in a type
that implements `Codec`, or send columnar data as Arrow.

Both ends are the same binary, so there's no versioning or schema.

modules.summary: A non-blocking framed connection, for the head's event loop.
modules.description:
The head talks to every driver and worker at once, so it must never block on
one of them. A `Conn` reads and writes with `MSG_DONTWAIT`, so no call
blocks. It reads whatever has arrived into an input buffer and
hands out complete frames, and queues outgoing frames in an output buffer
that `flush` drains as the socket accepts it. The event loop polls for
writability only while something is queued.

fields.name: closed
fields.summary: The peer hung up, or the connection failed.

overloads.signature: def read_available(mut self, limit: Int = Int(0))
overloads.summary: Reads what's waiting on the socket into the input buffer: all of it, or with `limit`, about that many bytes, leaving the rest in the socket, where `poll` still reports it.
The next complete frame in the input buffer, if there is one.

overloads.summary: Queues a frame and sends as much as the socket takes now.
Sends queued output until the socket would block.
Bytes queued to send that the peer hasn't taken yet.

modules.summary: Length-prefixed messages between drivers, the head and workers.
modules.description:
Every frame is a 4-byte little-endian length, then that many bytes:

| offset | field |
|---|---|
| 0 | kind (below) |
| 1 | object ID, u64 |
| 9 | task ID, u64 (0 unless the kind uses it) |
| 17 | payload |

| kind | sent by | payload |
|---|---|---|
| 1 task | driver to head, head to worker | the encoded argument |
| 2 result | worker to head, head to driver | the encoded result |
| 3 error | worker to head, head to driver | a UTF-8 message |
| 4 hello | driver, worker or observer to head | role byte (`ROLE_*`), the registry hash u64 (an observer's is ignored); a worker adds its object server's address |
| 5 welcome | head to driver | the driver's number, u64 |
| 6 task-after | driver to head | flags byte (`GATHER`, `WITH_VALUE`), count u64, then that many object IDs; with `WITH_VALUE`, a length u64 and the encoded value |
| 7 stored | worker to head | the result's size, u64: it stayed on the worker |
| 8 located | head to driver | the address of the worker holding the result |
| 9 fetch | driver or worker to a worker | none: send that object back as a result frame |
| 10 task-inputs | head to worker | flags byte, count u64, then per input a tag byte, its object ID, then for tag 0 a length u64 and the bytes, or for tag 1 its location; with `WITH_VALUE`, a length u64 and the value |
| 11 release | driver to head | none: the driver is done with this object |
| 12 free | head to worker | none: delete this object |
| 13 stats | driver to head, head to driver | none; the reply is five u64 counts (see `HeadStats`) |
| 14 holding | worker to head, on rejoining | count u64, then per object its ID u64 and its location |
| 15 claim | driver to head, on resuming | none: this driver still holds this object, which lives on a worker |
| 16 resumed | driver to head | none: this driver has restored, claimed or resubmitted everything |
| 17 span | worker to head, before the result | three u64 wall-clock nanoseconds: when the task arrived, started and ended |
| 18 timeline | driver to head, head to driver | none; the reply is a count u64, then per finished task its object ID, task ID, the four head stamps (submitted, queued, dispatched, settled), the three worker stamps, and the worker's address |
| 19 actor-create | driver to head, head to worker | from the driver, `checkpoint_every` u64 first; then the encoded constructor argument. The object ID names the actor, the task ID its type |
| 20 actor-call | driver to head, head to worker | the actor's ID u64, then the encoded argument; the task ID is the method's |
| 21 actor-kill | driver to head, head to worker | none: destroy the actor the object ID names |
| 22 checkpoint | driver to head, head to worker | from the driver, the actor's ID u64, and the object ID is the checkpoint's own; from the head, the calls covered by the checkpoint it would restore from, i64 (-1 for none), the object ID names the actor and the task ID is the number of calls the new one covers |
| 23 checkpointed | worker to head | none if the checkpoint is written, else why not; the object and task IDs are the checkpoint frame's |
| 24 actor-restore | head to worker | the number of calls the checkpoint covers, u64; the object ID names the actor, the task ID its type |
| 25 covered | head to driver | the newest of this driver's calls to the actor a checkpoint now includes, u64; the object ID names the actor |
| 26 status | observer to head, head to observer | none; the reply is the head's state as UTF-8 text |
| 27 stop | observer to head, head to worker | none: shut down; a worker exits instead of rejoining |
| 28 task-many | driver to head, head to worker | the number of results u64, then the encoded argument; the results are this object ID and the ones after it |
| 29 drain | worker to head | none: the worker was told to stop; it takes no more work, and leaves once the head says stop |
| 30 adopt | head to worker | a draining worker's location of the object: fetch it and keep it |
| 31 adopted | worker to head | 1 and the object's new location, or 0 and why not |

An observer (`dista status`, `timeline`, `stop`) says hello without a
registry and owns no objects. Its timeline frame gets every driver's
finished tasks, and leaves them for the drivers too.

After a head restart, a driver's hello carries its old number as a u64 after
the registry hash, so its object IDs stay valid. It then sends, in order of
submission, each object it still needs: a small result or error back as a
result or error frame, a result on a worker as claim, and an unfinished task
as the task or task-after frame it first sent; then resumed. A rejoining
worker sends holding.

An actor lives on one worker, which runs nothing else while it hosts it. The
worker answers actor-create with an empty result, or the constructor's
error, and each call like a task: a result, stored or error frame for the
call's object ID. Calls run in the order the driver sent them. A checkpoint
runs between calls too: the worker writes the actor's state to
`DISTA_CHECKPOINT_URI` and answers checkpointed. Actor-restore builds an
actor from its checkpoint instead of its constructor, and is answered like
actor-create.

Actors survive a head restart through their checkpoints. Every caller keeps
its calls to an actor until covered says a checkpoint includes them. A
resuming driver sends each live actor's actor-create again, in order with
everything else, then every call it still keeps: those answered too, after
their answers, since the actor's state hasn't seen them. The new head
restores the actor from its newest checkpoint; a call that checkpoint
already includes isn't run again. A rejoining worker destroys the actor it
hosted: its state may hold calls no caller would resend.

A task-after frame queues a task whose argument is built from other results:
the single result as is, or with gather set, a `Seq` of all of them; with
`WITH_VALUE` set, after an encoded value (a `TaskWith`). With `MANY` set it's
a `TaskMany`, whose results, the object ID and the ones after it, number the
u64 that follows the flags byte; the task-inputs frame carries it on.

A task-many frame runs a `TaskMany`: its worker answers each of its results
with its own result, stored or error frame, as if each were a task. When
some of those results live on workers, the head sends the task as
task-inputs, and the worker fetches them before it runs the task. An address
is 12 bytes: the IPv4 address, then the port as a u64.

The head counts references to every object: its driver's, until a release,
and one per submitted task that takes it as input, until that task settles.
At zero it forgets the object, and sends free to the worker holding it.

aliases.name: KIND_DRAIN
aliases.summary: Worker to head: it was told to stop (SIGTERM), so send it no more work and move what it holds; the head says `KIND_STOP` once it may go.

aliases.name: KIND_ADOPT
aliases.summary: Head to worker: fetch object `object_id` from the location in the payload, a draining worker's, and keep it as its own.

aliases.name: KIND_ADOPTED
aliases.summary: Worker to head: 1 and the object's new location, or 0 and why it couldn't take it.

aliases.name: GATHER
aliases.summary: Task-after and task-inputs flag: the inputs gather into a `Seq`.

aliases.name: WITH_VALUE
aliases.summary: Task-after and task-inputs flag: an encoded value goes before them.

aliases.name: MANY
aliases.summary: Task-after and task-inputs flag: the task is a `TaskMany`, and the number of its results, a u64, follows the flags byte.

aliases.name: ROLE_OBSERVER
aliases.summary: A driver inside a worker, for a task that calls actors: the head treats it as a driver, except that it doesn't keep a local-mode head alive.

modules.summary: The head: one event loop that schedules every driver's tasks onto workers.
modules.description:
Drivers and workers connect to the head and say hello with their role and
registry hash. A head built into a program refuses a peer whose hash isn't
its own, so every process runs the same tasks. A generic head (`dista head`,
registry hash 0) takes any, and hands a driver's tasks and actors only to
workers built from the same program, so one head serves several programs.
Observers (`dista status`, `timeline` and `stop`) say hello without a hash. A driver gets a number, which becomes the top bits of
every object ID it creates, so the head knows where each result goes.

The loop `poll`s the listener and every connection. Drivers send tasks, ready
to run or waiting on other results; the head queues them, hands them to
workers round-robin up to `pipeline` in flight each, and forwards each result
or error to the driver that owns it. A task whose inputs live mostly on one
node goes to a worker there when one is free (see `_pick`). Every socket is non-blocking with its
own output queue (`Conn`), so a slow peer can't stall anyone else.

Small results come through the head, which keeps them, because a task
submitted later may take one as input. A large result stays on the worker
that computed it: the head records where, tells the owning driver, and sends
a task that needs it as task-inputs, so the worker running that task fetches
it from its peer. A worker that goes away loses the results it held: dista
doesn't rebuild them (that's Ray's lineage reconstruction), so a task that
needs one fails, naming it, and an orchestrator runs the job again. The
tasks it was running are sent to another worker, up to `DISTA_TASK_RETRIES`
times (default 3), unless an input they read from that worker is gone too.

Submissions are admitted, not just accepted. While the tasks queued or
waiting on inputs reach `DISTA_MAX_QUEUED` (default 100,000), or their
arguments `DISTA_MAX_QUEUED_BYTES` (default 1 GiB), the head stops reading
from drivers. Their sockets fill, and `remote` blocks until workers drain the
queue: backpressure through TCP, with no frame of its own. Clients inside a
worker's task are read regardless, since pausing one would hold that worker,
and with every worker held, nothing would drain. 0 turns a limit off.

A driver that doesn't read what the head sends it, busy elsewhere, would
grow the head's output buffer by every result. Past `DISTA_MAX_DRIVER_BUFFER`
bytes waiting for it (default 256 MiB), its queued tasks aren't sent to
workers until it reads; its queue then fills, and admission control stops its
submissions. A driver waiting to submit reads meanwhile (see `Client`), so
this doesn't deadlock it.

Every object is reference counted: its driver holds it until it releases it
(or disconnects), and each submitted task taking it as input holds it until
that task settles. At zero the head forgets the object and tells the worker
holding it, if one does, to delete it. An object released before its task
finishes is freed when the task settles.

The head keeps nothing on disk. When it restarts, its state comes back from
its peers: workers rejoin and report the results they hold, and each driver
reconnects under its old number and restores, claims or resubmits everything
it still needs (see `frame.mojo`). A reported result no resumed driver
claimed is freed. A task that was running when the head died may run again.

A worker told to stop drains (see `worker.mojo`). The head sends it no more
tasks and has the other workers adopt every result it holds: each fetches
its copy, the head records where the result is now, and tells the driver
that owns it. A task sent the old location still finds the result, since the
draining worker keeps serving until it's gone. Once the worker runs no task
and holds nothing, the head lets it go, and it leaves without anything
failing or running again. An actor on a draining worker moves: the head
holds its new calls, asks for a checkpoint after the ones it sent, and once
that's written, restores the actor on another worker and sends the held
calls there, so none runs twice. Without `DISTA_CHECKPOINT_URI` the
checkpoint fails, and the actor restarts when its worker leaves, replaying
its calls, as for one lost.

An actor is placed on a worker that hosts no other, the one with the fewest
tasks in flight, as soon as it's created; the worker builds it once those
tasks finish. From then on the head sends that worker only the actor's calls,
each as it arrives, so they run in order. An actor created when every worker
hosts one waits for a worker to join or an actor to be killed. Killing an
actor, or its driver leaving, frees its worker for tasks.

The head keeps every call made to an actor since its last checkpoint. When
the actor's worker goes away, the actor is placed on another worker, built
again from that checkpoint, or from its constructor if it has none, and
those calls are run again in order, so its state is rebuilt: calls run at
least once. Each call is answered once: a call answered before the restart
keeps its first answer, and the replay's is dropped.

A checkpoint is asked for every `checkpoint_every` calls, if the actor was
created with one, and whenever a driver asks. The head sends it to the
actor's worker between calls, numbered by the calls it covers, and once the
worker says it's written, forgets the calls it covers, and tells each
caller the newest of its calls the checkpoint includes.

After a head restart, a resuming driver creates its actors again. The head
restores each from its newest checkpoint in `DISTA_CHECKPOINT_URI`, which
the head lists, or builds it if there's none, and the calls the callers
resend run on that: every call no checkpoint includes, answered or not.

With `DISTA_METRICS_PORT` set, the head and every worker answer HTTP on that
port with Prometheus's text format, which Kubernetes monitoring scrapes as it
is. It's off by default, since in local mode the head and its workers share
a host.

The server is the smallest one that does: the event loop polls its listener,
and each connection is answered on the spot. The request is read for up to
`READ_TIMEOUT_MS` and only its first line matters; every path gets the
metrics. A scrape is a few kilobytes, so answering it blocks the loop for
well under a millisecond, but a client that connects and sends nothing holds
it for the timeout.

modules.summary: The runtime: one binary that runs as driver, head or worker.
modules.description:
```mojo
comptime Square = Task[Int, Int, square]

def main() raises:
    var rt = Runtime[Square](workers=4)
    var r = rt.remote[Square](7)
    print(rt.get(r))  # 49
```

`Runtime(...)` reads the environment to decide what this process is:

| Environment | Role |
|---|---|
| `DISTA_ROLE=head` | runs the head on `DISTA_PORT` (default 6390) and never returns |
| `DISTA_ROLE=worker` | serves the head at `DISTA_HEAD=host:port` and never returns |
| `DISTA_HEAD=host:port` | a driver that submits to that head |
| neither | local mode: forks a head and `workers` workers, then drives them |

So a cluster runs one image everywhere, and the same program runs on a laptop
unchanged. The registry is the runtime's parameter list: workers dispatch
with a `comptime for` over it, and every process's hello carries a hash of it
so the head refuses a mismatched build.

A driver sends tasks to the head and reads results back. Small results come
with the reply; a large one stays on the worker that computed it. On the same
host `get` maps it from the node store and decodes it in place; from another
host it fetches it from that worker directly. A task can take
another task's result: pass an `ObjectRef[A]` instead of an `A`, or a
`List[ObjectRef[X]]` to a task that takes a `Seq[X]`. The head runs it once
every input exists, and fails it if an input failed.

`create` starts an actor on a worker of its own and returns its handle;
`call` runs one of its methods there, in the order of the calls, and returns
an `ObjectRef` like a task does; `checkpoint` saves its state to
`DISTA_CHECKPOINT_URI`; `kill` destroys it.

modules.summary: How many workers a running job wants: a policy over the head's demand.
modules.description:
dista starts no machines. Whatever owns them (orca's `ec2` runner, a shell
loop, a Kubernetes operator) reads the head's demand, `dista status --json`,
asks `decide` what to do, starts that many workers and drains the ones it
names with `dista drain`:

    var d = Demand.parse(observer.status_json())
    var got = decide(d, Policy(min_workers=0, max_workers=12), now, pending,
                     short_since)
    # start got.start workers; drain each of got.drain; keep got.short_since

`decide` has no clock and no I/O: `now` is the provider's, in seconds, and
`short_since`, when the job first ran short of workers, comes back in the
decision for the next call. So it's tested on tables of demand over time.

Up: tasks ready with no free slot for `up_after` seconds start workers, at
most `max_step` at once, up to `max_workers`; with no worker at all, they
start at once. Workers asked for but not yet joined (`pending`) count as
there, so a slow boot isn't asked for twice.

Down: workers idle for `idle_before_down` seconds drain, fewest held bytes
first, down to `min_workers`, which may be 0. A worker hosting an actor
drains only with a checkpoint store to move it through; and the last worker
drains only once no task is left and it holds nothing, since its results
would have nowhere to go.

modules.summary: `Seq[T]`: a list that goes through the codec.
modules.description:
`List` can't be encoded by reflection, because reflection can't recover its
element type. `Seq[T]` carries `T` as a parameter, so it can encode each
element with the generic codec:

```mojo
def total(xs: Seq[Int]) -> Int:
    var t = 0
    for i in range(len(xs)):
        t += xs[i]
    return t

comptime Total = Task[Seq[Int], Int, total]
```

On the wire a `Seq` is an 8-byte count, then each element's encoding. That is
also how the runtime builds one from a list of `ObjectRef`s: the count, then
each result's bytes as they arrived, without decoding them.

modules.summary: SIGTERM: the head exits, and a worker drains, even as a container's PID 1.
modules.description:
Kubernetes stops a pod with SIGTERM, and the kernel drops any signal sent to
a container's PID 1, as dista's process is, unless it has a handler for it.
The head's handler exits at once, as the signal's default action would. A
worker's writes a byte to a pipe its event loop polls, so the worker can
drain: finish what it's running, hand what it holds to other workers, and
leave (see `worker.mojo`). A second SIGTERM, or one that arrives before the
worker's loop runs, ends it at once.

A signal handler can't reach a Mojo variable, so the pipe's write end is
duplicated onto a fixed descriptor, `WAKE_FD`, which the handler writes to.

Both ends block (setting O_NONBLOCK needs a variadic `fcntl`, which `external_call` can't make on Apple's arm64), so read it only once `poll` says it's readable.

Just enough of `socket(2)` and friends for dista's processes: listeners on
loopback or on every interface, streams to a host name or to loopback, the
non-blocking reads and writes the head's event loop uses, `poll`, and
`fork`/`waitpid`/`_exit` to start and reap local processes. macOS and Linux
differ in `sockaddr_in`'s first byte, in `addrinfo`'s field order, in the
`SOL_SOCKET`, `MSG_DONTWAIT` and `EAGAIN` constants, and in how a write to a
closed peer is kept from raising SIGPIPE; `platform_map` picks the right value
for each.

modules.summary: The node-local object store: large results in shared mappings.
modules.description:
A worker writes each large result into a file in a node-local directory
(`/dev/shm` on Linux, `$TMPDIR` on macOS, or `DISTA_STORE_DIR`). A reader
that can see that file maps it, through memory-region's `SharedMapping`,
read-only and reads the bytes where they lie: no socket, no copy through
the kernel's network stack. A reader that can't fetches the result over a
socket from the worker, as before.

"Can see the file" is the test, not a matching host name: file names carry a
random token per worker, so a file with the right name is the right file.
That covers one machine, and Kubernetes pods that share a volume. (Host
names turned out to be unreliable: on GitHub's macOS runners, processes on
one machine reported different ones.)

`DISTA_SHM=0` turns the store off; large results then stay in the worker's
memory and are always fetched over sockets.

Spilling: a worker keeps at most `DISTA_STORE_BYTES` of results in the store
(no limit when unset), and a result past that, or one the store can't take,
goes to `DISTA_SPILL_DIR` on disk instead (default `$TMPDIR`, or `/tmp`).
A spilled result is read the same way, mapped or fetched, only from disk.
On Kubernetes `/dev/shm` is an in-memory volume whose size limit evicts the
pod rather than failing a write, so the limit is what keeps it in bounds.

A location says where a result is: the worker's object server address, its
host name, the file's path ("" when it's only in memory) and the exact size,
since mapped files are padded.

modules.summary: Tasks: remote functions, their IDs, and how a worker runs one.
modules.description:
A task wraps a top-level `def` with its argument and result types:

```mojo
def square(x: Int) -> Int:
    return x * x

comptime Square = Task[Int, Int, square]
```

The types are spelled out because Mojo can't infer a function's result type
from the function value. The function may raise or not; both bind to
`def(A) thin raises -> R`.

Every node runs the same binary, so a task message names the task by ID: a
64-bit FNV-1a hash of the function's linkage name, which includes its module
and argument types. The hash is fixed, unlike `hash()`, so a driver and a
worker started separately agree on it.

An actor is a state type and the function that builds it, and each of its
methods is a function taking the state `mut`:

```mojo
def new_counter(start: Int) -> Counter:
    return Counter(start)

def add(mut c: Counter, n: Int) -> Int:
    c.total += n
    return c.total

comptime CounterActor = Actor[Counter, Int, new_counter]
comptime Add = Method[CounterActor, Int, Int, add]
```

Actors and methods go in the runtime's registry with the tasks. The worker
hosting an actor keeps its state behind a `StatePtr`, which only the actor's
own `create`, `destroy`, `save` and `restore` and its methods' `call` cast
back to its type. A checkpoint is the state through the codec, so a state
type that implements `Codec` chooses what it saves.

modules.summary: A worker: runs tasks for the head and serves its results to peers.
modules.description:
A small result (up to `INLINE_LIMIT` bytes) goes back to the head, which
forwards it. A larger one stays here: in a shared mapping in the node's store
(see `store.mojo`), or in memory if the store is off. The worker tells the
head where it is; a reader on this host maps the file, and one elsewhere
fetches it from this worker's object server.

So a worker is an event loop over the head, its listener, the drivers and
workers fetching from it, and the workers it fetches from. A task whose
inputs live on other workers waits, parked, until they've all arrived; the
worker keeps serving fetches meanwhile. No worker ever waits on another one
synchronously, so two workers that need each other's results can't deadlock.
Running a task does block the loop, so fetches from this worker wait until
the current task finishes.

A result here lives until the head says free, once nothing references it.
Inputs fetched from peers are copies, kept only until the tasks waiting on
them have their arguments.

A worker the head gives an actor builds its state and then runs only that
actor's calls, in the order they come. A kill destroys the state, and the
worker goes back to running tasks. Between calls the head may ask for a
checkpoint: the worker writes the state through the codec to
`DISTA_CHECKPOINT_URI` (see `checkpoint.mojo`), and deletes the checkpoint
before it. An actor restarted elsewhere is restored from the last one.

A worker told to stop (SIGTERM, as Kubernetes sends) drains: it tells the
head, which sends it no more work and has other workers adopt the results it
holds, each fetching its copy from here. It finishes what it was given, and
once the head says stop, it serves fetches a moment longer, for tasks given
its old locations, and exits. `DISTA_DRAIN_SECONDS` (default 25, inside
Kubernetes' default grace period of 30) bounds the whole drain.

If the head goes away, `run` returns and the results here stay. `rejoin`
introduces the worker to a new head and reports what it holds; the tasks it
had queued are dropped, since their drivers resubmit them. An actor it
hosted is destroyed: actors don't survive a head restart yet, though their
checkpoints stay.

aliases.summary: How long a drained worker keeps serving fetches after the head says stop: a task sent before its inputs moved may still fetch them from here.
